title: Recollecting virtue
hookLine: a robe is being sewn for a journey, and a lay follower asks how to live once the teacher is gone
tomorrow: how can giving something away be a gain for you?

cards: A going-away gift says the thing nobody wants to say out loud: someone is leaving. In one sutta, monks are sewing a new robe for the Buddha, and a finished robe means he'll soon set out walking.
Mahanama the Sakyan, a lay follower, hears about the sewing and understands. He comes with the question under all those needles.
We who live in all sorts of ways, with houses and work and families: when you go, how should we live? The answer begins with three names anyone would expect. Then it does something strange.
It tells Mahanama to remember himself.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA, THE TEACHING, THE COMMUNITY.
teach.b: The Buddha gives Mahanama things to call to mind. The Buddha. The teaching.
And fourth: your own virtue. Not a saint's. Yours.
Recall the precepts you've kept, he says, kept whole, unbroken, unstained, the kind the wise would praise. Then he lays out what happens next, like a chain.
When you remember that, the mind isn't taken over by greed, or hate, or confusion.
It goes straight. Gladness comes, and out of gladness, joy. The body calms.
A calm body feels at ease, and a mind at ease settles.

Buddhaghosa's meditation manual, the Visuddhimagga, turns this into a subject of its own: sit, and go over your conduct gladly. That last word does the work. This isn't a résumé, and nobody else needs to hear it.
It's closer to the quiet at the end of a day when you told the truth and it cost you something. The texts are speaking to someone whose conduct is clean.
If yours has a smudge, one answer in the tradition is plain: take the precepts again, keep them, and then there's something to remember.
Glad of my conduct, and no trace of showing off.

how: Lay Buddhists take the five precepts at temple gatherings and on observance days, and Theravada teachers give the recollection of virtue as a quiet meditation on precepts kept.

o: praising a saint's good deeds out loud
listing your faults so you can fix them
calling your own good conduct to mind, gladly

games.q: who did what, and what follows — tap the pairs.
p: asks how to live once the Buddha leaves
a sign the Buddha will set out
the fourth thing to call to mind

s: remembering your own good deeds is just bragging
it's done privately and gladly; nobody else needs to hear it.
in the sutta, a mind recalling its virtue isn't taken over by greed, hate or confusion
it goes straight, and gladness, joy, calm and ease follow, like links in a chain.
the recollection is only for people who never did anything wrong
the texts speak to a clean conscience; one answer in the tradition is to take the precepts again and keep them.

games.q: you kept a hard promise to a friend, and you keep replaying it at night, quietly glad. someone says that's just ego. what does the manual say?
o: they're right: dwelling on your own good is self-centered.
recall it gladly; that gladness is how the mind settles.
it only counts if somebody else noticed and praised it.
games.why: the Visuddhimagga makes this a meditation: go over your conduct gladly. the chain runs from gladness to joy, calm, ease and a settled mind.

practice: Find one time you did the decent thing when it would have been easier not to: the truth told, the wallet handed back, the cruel joke you didn't make.
Write it as one short line, on paper if you have some, and rest your eyes on that line for the sit. If gladness comes, let it stay; if it doesn't, the remembering is enough.

wordCard.voice: Recollecting virtue: calling your own good conduct to mind, gladly, as a meditation. The fourth thing the Buddha told Mahanama to remember.

orig.note: Pali: sila, virtue or conduct, with anussati, recollection, calling to mind.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: glad of my conduct, the quiet kind of glad. Twenty-two days into the forty subjects.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 11.11 (Mahanama Sutta: the robe being made; Mahanama asks how to dwell; six recollections, the fourth being one's own virtue)
Anguttara Nikaya 6.10 (recollecting virtue: unbroken, untorn, praised by the wise; the mind goes straight; gladness, joy, calm, ease, concentration)
